cues.text: Section eleven: IT project management.
Let us begin with a basic distinction.
A project is a temporary endeavour that produces a unique outcome.
Operations, by contrast, are ongoing activities that sustain services.
Deploying a new ERP system is a project.
Supporting that ERP after launch is operations.
IT projects face a particular set of pressures: changing requirements, technical dependencies, uncertainty, integration risks, security constraints and stakeholder expectations.
Project management is the discipline that coordinates scope, time, cost, quality, resources, risks and communication, so that the agreed outcomes are achieved.
Now to the main delivery approaches.
Waterfall is a predictive approach.
It uses planned, sequential phases, such as requirements, design, implementation, testing and deployment.
It suits situations where requirements are stable and where there is a strong need for documentation.
Its weakness is that it can be costly to change direction late in the project.
Agile is an adaptive approach.
It emphasises iterative delivery, feedback and responsiveness.
Scrum is an Agile framework, and it uses sprints, a product backlog, sprint planning, the daily Scrum, the sprint review and the retrospective.
The Scrum Team includes a Product Owner, a Scrum Master and Developers.
Kanban is another approach: it visualises work, limits work in progress, and improves flow.
Hybrid delivery combines predictive and adaptive practices.
For example, a regulated banking project may use formal approval gates and architecture planning, while still delivering the software in iterations.
Note that hybrid is not simply using random tools.
The practices chosen should fit the project's constraints.
Next, planning.
Planning starts with objectives, scope and acceptance criteria.
A work breakdown structure, or WBS, decomposes deliverables into manageable pieces of work.
A schedule identifies dependencies, milestones and resources.
A Gantt chart visualises activities over time.
And the critical path is the longest-duration dependency path, which determines the earliest possible project completion.
Let us work through an example.
Requirements take three days.
Backend development takes five days.
Integration testing takes two days.
Frontend development takes four days, and it can run alongside the backend after requirements are done.
Integration waits for both.
So the earliest completion is three, plus the larger of five and four, plus two, which equals ten days.
The backend path is the critical path, and under these assumptions the frontend has one day of float.
Several other artefacts support execution: risk registers, communication plans, budgets, quality plans and assignments of responsibility.
During the project, you monitor actual progress against baselines, investigate any deviations, and approve scope changes properly, rather than silently expanding commitments.
Now an earned value example.
Three terms first.
Planned value, or PV, is the budgeted work that was scheduled.
Earned value, or EV, is the budgeted value of the work actually completed.
Actual cost, or AC, is the expenditure incurred.
Suppose planned value is ten million naira, earned value is eight million naira, and actual cost is nine million naira.
Schedule variance, or SV, equals EV minus PV.
That is minus two million naira, which means the project is behind the planned work.
Cost variance, or CV, equals EV minus AC.
That is minus one million naira, which means the project is over budget for the work completed.
The schedule performance index, or SPI, equals EV divided by PV, which is zero point eight.
The cost performance index, or CPI, equals EV divided by AC, which is approximately zero point eight nine.
A caution on these measures.
They depend on reliable estimates of completed work, and they do not directly predict calendar delays.
So use them alongside quality, risks and stakeholder feedback.
Finally, closing a project.
You close a project by verifying acceptance, handing over documentation and support responsibilities, reviewing lessons learned, and evaluating the benefits that were actually realised.
